questions.prompt: Which HTTP status code specifically means a POST request succeeded and created a new resource?
options: 200 OK
201 Created
204 No Content
400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
404 Not Found
questions.explain: 201 Created is the status code that specifically confirms a POST succeeded and a new resource now exists. It falls in the 2xx success range, like 200, but carries the more specific meaning of 'created.'
questions.distractorExplain: 200 OK is the closest wrong answer because it's also a 2xx success code, but it's the generic 'the read succeeded' response most associated with GET. It doesn't carry the specific 'a new resource now exists' meaning that 201 does, which is the detail this question is testing.

questions.prompt: An integration developer wants to look up one existing invoice whose ID is 300000182. Based on how REST organizes resources around URLs, which request is correct?
options: GET /fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/invoices/300000182
GET /fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/invoices?id=300000182
POST /fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/invoices with the ID placed in the request body
GET /fscmRestApi/resources/11.13.18.05/getInvoiceById/300000182
questions.explain: REST addresses a specific resource instance by appending its ID directly to the collection's URL, so /invoices/300000182 is the invoice itself. Inventing a query parameter, using POST for a read, or inventing a custom action-name endpoint all contradict REST's resource-and-verb convention.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: because Oracle Fusion's REST API is ________, every single request must carry everything the server needs, including authentication, since the server remembers nothing from the previous call.
questions.explain: Statelessness means the server treats every request independently — nothing is remembered between calls, so each one must be fully self-contained, credentials included.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 1 term to what it actually means.
right: An architectural style for designing APIs around resources
A 3-digit number telling you whether, and how, a request succeeded
A documented way for one program to request data or action from another
A lightweight, text-based format most REST APIs use for requests and responses
questions.explain: API is the general concept of a documented door between programs; REST is the specific architectural style Oracle Fusion's APIs follow; JSON is the text format those calls send and receive; a status code is the 3-digit result the server hands back.

questions.prompt: Put these steps for safely using Oracle Fusion's REST API documentation before sending a POST, in the correct order.
items: Find the resource's documentation page for the Fusion release you're targeting
Confirm the method and path listed for the operation you need
Review the request body schema to see which fields are required
Check the example payload for a worked sample request
Send the request only after the required fields are confirmed
questions.explain: Reading documentation always runs from general to specific: find the right page for your release, confirm the method and path, check which fields the schema actually requires, look at a worked example, and only then send the request. Skipping the required-fields check is the most common avoidable cause of a 400 error.

questions.prompt: A production integration currently calls /fscmRestApi/resources/latest/invoices. What is the main risk of this, compared to pointing at a fixed version string like 11.13.18.05?
options: "latest" always resolves to whatever is newest, so a future Fusion update could silently change the resource's shape underneath the integration
"latest" cannot be used with the invoices resource at all
"latest" always points to an older, deprecated version of the resource
"latest" requires a completely different authentication method than a fixed version string does
questions.explain: A fixed version string stays stable even as Oracle updates the environment, while "latest" always resolves to whatever is newest — convenient for exploring, but risky for production because an update could change the resource's shape out from under an integration that assumed nothing would change.

questions.prompt: Given the response shown above, what should the next request do to retrieve the following page of invoices?
options: Repeat the same request with limit=100 and offset=100
Repeat the exact same request unchanged — Fusion automatically advances to the next page on its own
Send a POST request carrying the same filter to advance the page
Increase limit to a very large number so hasMore becomes false on the next call
questions.explain: The paging pattern is to keep the same limit and increase offset by that same amount on each subsequent call, repeating until hasMore comes back false. Fusion does not advance pages on its own between identical requests.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about creating and updating Oracle Fusion Financials records via REST, per Chapter 2.
options: POST targets the collection URL, because the record being created doesn't have an ID yet
PATCH targets the specific record's own URL
PATCH requires resending every field on the record, not just the ones actually changing
Both POST and PATCH need a Content-Type: application/json header
DELETE is the standard, encouraged way to remove a posted financial record
questions.explain: POST creates at the collection URL since there's no ID yet, and PATCH updates a specific record at its own URL, changing only the fields included in the body — not the whole record. Both need Content-Type: application/json. DELETE is rarely permitted on financial records, not a standard removal path.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in an Oracle Fusion REST list response, the ________ flag tells you whether more records exist beyond the current page.
questions.explain: hasMore is the flag in a list response that tells you whether to keep paging. When it's true, more records exist beyond what you just received; when false, you've reached the end of the result set.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 2 term to what it actually does.
right: Pulls a related child resource into the same response
A predefined, named lookup with its own bind parameters
A filter expression using operators like =, >=, and LIKE
A tool like Postman or curl for building and testing HTTP requests directly
questions.explain: q is the general-purpose filter expression, finder is a predefined named lookup for conditions q can't express, expand pulls a child resource into the same response, and a REST client is the tool used to build and test any of these calls directly.

questions.prompt: What does a 401 status code mean when Oracle Fusion's REST API returns it?
options: Authentication failed, or credentials are missing
Authentication succeeded, but authorization denied the action
The requested resource doesn't exist
The request body was malformed
The server encountered an unexpected internal error
The request was rejected for exceeding a rate limit
questions.explain: A 401 means the server could not confirm who you are — authentication itself failed or was never attempted (missing or invalid credentials). This check happens before Fusion ever evaluates what that identity would be allowed to do.
questions.distractorExplain: 403 Forbidden (authorization succeeded, access denied) is the closest wrong answer, and it's easy to conflate the two since both sound like 'access denied.' But 403 means your identity WAS proven and then denied a specific action, while 401 means identity was never successfully proven in the first place — a meaningfully earlier failure point.

questions.prompt: A developer argues that Basic Authentication is secure because the credentials are base64-encoded before being sent. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Base64 is reversible encoding, not encryption — anyone who intercepts it can decode the original username and password almost instantly
Base64-encoded credentials automatically expire after a short time, so interception doesn't actually matter
Base64 encoding is only used by OAuth 2.0, never by Basic Authentication
Base64 encoding prevents the Authorization header from being read by anything except Oracle Fusion's own servers
questions.explain: Base64 is a reversible text encoding, not encryption. It makes the credentials look obscured, but anyone who intercepts the header can decode it back to the plain username and password almost instantly. The actual protection comes from sending every call over HTTPS, not from the encoding itself.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about setting up a dedicated integration user for a system-to-system integration, per Chapter 3.
options: It should be scoped with only the specific job/duty roles the integration actually needs
It should reuse a current employee's personal login so it's easy to track who it belongs to
It should be read-only if the integration only ever reads data
Its password rotation and access review should be owned centrally by IT/security, not left to one individual
It should be granted broad administrative access up front, in case future requirements expand
questions.explain: A properly configured integration user follows least privilege: only the roles it needs, read-only when it only reads, with lifecycle ownership held centrally by IT/security. Reusing a personal login is exactly the failure mode this lesson warns against, and granting broad access 'just in case' is the opposite of least privilege.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: rather than retrying a failed call immediately, a well-built integration waits progressively longer between attempts — a strategy called exponential ________.
questions.explain: Exponential backoff waits progressively longer between retry attempts (for example 1s, 2s, 4s) rather than hammering a struggling server immediately after each failure.

questions.prompt: Put these diagnostic steps for a failing Oracle Fusion REST call in the correct order, based on Chapter 3.
items: Check whether the status code falls in the 4xx or 5xx range
If it's a 401, confirm the credentials and authentication method before anything else
If it's a 403 instead, check the integration user's assigned roles and access rather than its credentials
If it's a 429, 500, or 503, retry with exponential backoff rather than treating it as a hard failure
questions.explain: Diagnosis starts broad (which range is it in?) and narrows from there: a 401 points to authentication, a 403 points to authorization/roles instead, and only the genuinely transient codes (429, 500, 503) are worth an exponential-backoff retry at all.

questions.prompt: A client needs 20,000 legacy AP invoices loaded once at go-live, with no ongoing need for that volume afterward. Which integration pattern best fits, and why?
options: Batch/bulk — a one-time, high-volume load is exactly what a scheduled bulk pattern is built for
Real-time REST — because REST calls are always faster, regardless of volume
Event-driven — because a business event could be configured to fire 20,000 times in sequence
None of the three patterns fit; a one-time load always requires custom scripting outside of these patterns
questions.explain: Volume, latency, and frequency decide the pattern. A large one-time load with no ongoing recurrence is exactly the scenario batch/bulk integration is designed for — real-time REST and event-driven both fit recurring, per-transaction scenarios instead, not a single large historical load.

questions.prompt: A BI tool calls GET /journals every night to pull GL balances into a corporate data warehouse. How should this integration be classified?
options: Outbound, because an external system is reading data out of Fusion
Inbound, because the extracted data ends up stored in another system
Event-driven, because it happens automatically every night without a person triggering it
It can't be classified without first knowing the integration's data volume
questions.explain: Direction is about which way data moves, not where it ends up or how automated it is. An external system calling GET against Fusion is reading data out — that's outbound, by the same rule of thumb that an external system calling POST/PATCH is writing data in, or inbound.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Oracle Integration Cloud (OIC) and business events, per Chapter 4.
options: OIC's ERP Cloud adapter already understands how to talk to Fusion Financials' REST resources
An OIC integration flow consists of a trigger, a transform step, and a delivery step
Business events are enabled by default for every Financials module
OIC can subscribe to a specific Fusion business event through its ERP Cloud adapter
Polling and event-driven integration are two different names for the same underlying mechanism
questions.explain: OIC's ERP Cloud adapter is the built-in bridge to Fusion's REST resources, and every OIC flow breaks down into trigger, transform, and deliver. OIC can subscribe to a business event through that same adapter. Business events are NOT on by default — they require an explicit 'Enable Business Events' profile option per module — and polling/event-driven are genuinely different mechanisms with different latency and call-volume characteristics.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a system-generated notification that Oracle Fusion raises at a specific lifecycle moment, such as an invoice being approved, is called a ________.
questions.explain: A business event is Fusion announcing that something happened the instant it happens, so a subscriber like OIC can react immediately instead of repeatedly polling to check for changes.

questions.prompt: Match each financial data exchange scenario to its typical direction and pattern, per Lesson 19's recap.
questions.explain: A bank statement feed typically creates records inside Fusion on a batch schedule (inbound, batch). A tax engine lookup happens per transaction as data leaves Fusion (outbound, real-time). An expense system feed creates records inside Fusion as they occur (inbound, real-time or event-driven). A consolidation extract reads large volumes out of Fusion on a schedule (outbound, batch) — none of these are rigid rules, but they are the typical shape each scenario takes based on volume, latency, and frequency.
